messages.author: 5f4538afa2f74b06
messages.subject: Newbie questions
parts:
Ey folks,

 

I'm a newbie in SCR analysis, I and would like to comment a couple of thought after my first oSCR analysis.

 

First, I would like to congrats anyone involved for the oSCR package, vignettes and youtube channel. It is pretty well documented everything.

Now the questions:

 1)      The first one is related to the pixel resolution. My states pace area was defined from a polygon. My target species is roe deer, and the study area is fenced, so the state space area is limited by the fenced area, and I don't consider 3*sigma to define the buffer area because I assumed that animals can't cross fences (gamekeepers also assumed that). In this respect, and following the vignette (https://bookdown.org/chrissuthy/oSCRvignettes/objects.html#creating-statespace-from-a-polygon) I considered a sigma=0.5 (km) to define the potential activity centres (estimated sigma was 0.6km in the analysis):

#Code:
buff <- 0
# Create state-space from study area and buffer
ss_polygon <- st_buffer(study_area, dist = buff)
sigma <- 0.5
ssgrid_size <- as.numeric(round((st_area(ss_polygon)/1000^2) / sigma^2))
ss_points <- st_sample(x = ss_polygon, size = ssgrid_size, type = "regular")

 

After that, these are the plots of the best model (attached)


Checking the realized density plot, I’m concerned about the pixel resolution, because of the high difference in density between two adjacent pixels (see the green ones in the left part for instance). In your examples, the differences between pixels are smoothed. And my question is: it is necessary to consider a lower pixel size? If I’m right, pixel resolution should be lower than sigma, and in my data it is (pixel=0.5km, sigma=0.6km)….

 

2)     Second, as results are sensitive to ssDF definition; it is correct my procedure to define the space state area based on the fenced limits? Some of my traps (cameras in this case) are very close to the limits (even < sigma), so, if I’m right, don’t make sense to consider 3*sigma as buffer area if there is a physical fence that animal cannot cross. Additionally,  should I discard some areas within the fenced area since they are too far from the traps? (for example north corner, or central-left part in my plot). If I discard those areas that take the mean density value as density value, the abundance will change...

Thank you very much for your help

All the best

Pablo

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [oscr] Newbie questions
parts:
hi Pablo,
 I agree it is a little weird to see the highest density values surrounded by the lowest values... not sure exactly what to make of that.  I do agree that perhaps a smaller pixel size is needed (0.25 might be ok).  But I don't think it will change the map too much or at least it shouldn't. You do have a peculiar situation with the constrained state-space and a lot of individuals it seems with no recaptures.  I would be curious to see the result when you don't use a constrained state-space (but I think it is wise to use the constrained state-space). 
 If possible please post the model fit results.
regards
andy

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: [oscr] Newbie questions
parts:
To add a few more thoughts:

1) Remember that when you specify constant density (D~1), you are assuming that each pixel has the same expected value. This forces the realized map to have highs and lows, sometimes extreme, to accommodate the fact that your capture data indicate a pattern where some pixels definitely/probably have individuals. In order to even out the predictions, some pixels will therefore need to have zero (or a much lower realized value). These concepts aren’t intuitive and often cause confusion.

That said, you could decrease your state space resolution incrementally until the model estimates reach agreement to find the optimal resolution. But I agree with Andy that it’s unlikely to make a huge difference here with these sparse data.

2) If you have hard boundaries that individuals cannot cross (e.g., an effective fence), it makes sense to restrict the state space even if traps were near the edge. But pixels that are too far from traps (having p=0 essentially) are trickier to handle depending on the context. Those pixels or areas of the state space may not affect model estimates but would certainly affect derived population or abundance, like you said. I’d be inclined to keep them so that your N estimate is “for the fenced area”, recognizing there is great uncertainty in the untrapped areas. But it really depends on your objectives, like most things.

parts:
Dear Andy and Daniel,

Thank you very much for your constructive comments.

Following your suggestions, I have considered pixels of 100m; and I have compared the fenced-area model, with the 4*sigma buffer for the state-space model. Here the results (and plot attached):

# FENCED AREA MODEL
Model: D ~ 1 p0 ~ 1 sig ~ 1
Run time: 28.3355 minutes
AIC: 857.8779
Summary table:
                         Estimate   SE       z         P(>|z|)
p0.(Intercept) -1.184   0.380   -3.118    0.002
sig.(Intercept) 6.301   0.072   87.851   0.000
d0.(Intercept) -5.962   0.292   -20.438  0.000
*Density intercept is log(individuals per pixel)
Nhat(state-space) = exp(d0.)*nrow(ssDF)
(caution is warranted when model contains density covariates)

# 4*SIGMA BUFFER MODEL
Model: D ~ 1 p0 ~ 1 sig ~ 1
Run time: 26.8455 minutes
AIC: 840.2209
Summary table:
                         Estimate   SE      z        P(>|z|)
p0.(Intercept) -0.844   0.371   -2.272    0.023
sig.(Intercept) 6.328   0.074    86.076   0.000
d0.(Intercept) -6.260   0.295   -21.215   0.000
*Density intercept is log(individuals per pixel)
Nhat(state-space) = exp(d0.)*nrow(ssDF)
(caution is warranted when model contains density covariates)

I included the null model for simplicity (at this point). Now I'm concerned about the south-area results. The spider plot (attached) showed that two animals were captured on the cameras placed on the left-bottom corner. However, the realized density there were 0. So there should be an error when importing the data into the models... Don't make sense that if animals were captured, density is 0, right? (for more details, 12 captures of one animal were recorded in camera 10; and 5 captures of another animal were recorded in camera 11).

Working on the error...

Thanks again
Best
Pablo

messages.subject: Re: [oscr] Newbie questions
parts:
Those model comparisons suggest not much change between the parameter estimates, but there also isn’t a metric to suggest one is more appropriate than the other. If you have a fence that works, then the restricted state space is probably more logical.

As for the realized density, I’d first advocate caution in interpretation. More importantly, it does make sense that the pixels with traps have low density estimates because the model is suggesting that capture probability is low enough such that your observed captures are likely from individuals with activity centers located away from the trap locations. Again, this is not intuitive but it is consistent with what is often seen in these models, especially with sparse encounter histories.

To add a few more thoughts:

1) Remember that when you specify constant density (D~1), you are assuming that each pixel has the same expected value. This forces the realized map to have highs and lows, sometimes extreme, to accommodate the fact that your capture data indicate a pattern where some pixels definitely/probably have individuals. In order to even out the predictions, some pixels will therefore need to have zero (or a much lower realized value). These concepts aren’t intuitive and often cause confusion.

That said, you could decrease your state space resolution incrementally until the model estimates reach agreement to find the optimal resolution. But I agree with Andy that it’s unlikely to make a huge difference here with these sparse data.

2) If you have hard boundaries that individuals cannot cross (e.g., an effective fence), it makes sense to restrict the state space even if traps were near the edge. But pixels that are too far from traps (having p=0 essentially) are trickier to handle depending on the context. Those pixels or areas of the state space may not affect model estimates but would certainly affect derived population or abundance, like you said. I’d be inclined to keep them so that your N estimate is “for the fenced area”, recognizing there is great uncertainty in the untrapped areas. But it really depends on your objectives, like most things.
